definition: Truth as a substantive property: a sentence is true when it represents things as they are, and only sentences that state how things are (truth-apt sentences) can be true. O'Connor's 'no truth value: not the kind of sentence that can be true or false' denies moral statements truth in this sense; `Holds` in the emotivism results is truth in this sense. In the van Roojen readings, `RobustlyTruthApt φ` is aptness for truth in this sense: 'robust truth or falsity', 'substantial truth conditions' (SEP §1.1), as opposed to minimal truth-aptness (DEF-MINIMAL-TRUTH-APTNESS).
note: The robust/minimal contrast is the project's label from the debate on truth minimalism (Horwich, Wright, Blackburn). The SEP entry 'Moral Cognitivism vs. Non-Cognitivism' (pinned as a web snapshot) uses the contrast (§1.1, preamble, §5.2) but does not define robust truth beyond 'substantial'; that 'robust' adds representation of how things are is this record's stipulation. Dreier's criterion (STMT-ROBUST-MORAL-TRUTH-IS-EXPLANATORY) is a proposed mark of it, kept as a separate premise, not part of the definition. The sourced content it labels for the emotivism results is O'Connor's gloss (claim OCONNOR-DESTINY-ETHICS-NOT-TRUE-OR-FALSE).
